commons:98691704.summary: In the gold-ground medallion at the summit of the dome, John the Baptist stands on a rocky bank and baptizes Christ, who stands waist-deep in the Jordan while the dove of the Holy Spirit descends above him. At the right sits the personified river Jordan, a figure borrowed from classical river gods, as if witnessing the scene. Set directly above the font where Ravenna's Christians were baptized, the image showed every neophyte the event their own baptism repeated. It is one of the earliest monumental baptism scenes to survive in its original place.
facts: The octagonal baptistery was erected under Bishop Ursus around 400 and completed, with its mosaic decoration, under Bishop Neon later in the 5th century, which gives the building its name.

Christ's and the Baptist's faces, the dove and the jewelled cross are not original: Italian Wikipedia records that they were remade in a later (18th-century) restoration, so the central group is partly a modern reconstruction.
The medallion is surrounded by a procession of the twelve apostles, and the baptistery is one of the eight Early Christian monuments of Ravenna inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

commons:98691704.notes: Date: Commons/Wikidata give 5th century; mosaics added under Bishop Neon (bishop c. 450–473). Not already in c-2…c-11 (no Neon Baptistery entry found). Sources differ on whether the heads were remade in the 18th or 19th century; the fact is phrased after Italian Wikipedia.

cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-amiens-chris.summary: In this copy from the abbey of Corbie, Christ again stands with arms outstretched across a framed grid of letters, his cross-nimbus inscribed and his long hair and beard drawn in dark ink; the outlines of his body enclose separate verses within the poem. The red loincloth and simple flesh tones make the figure stand out from the even field of capitals.
facts: Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda and later Archbishop of Mainz, composed this cycle of figure-poems (carmina figurata) in praise of the Cross around 810; each page is a grid of letters in which shapes pick out further verses.
This manuscript came from the abbey of Corbie and is now in the municipal library of Amiens; it was digitised for the Europeana Regia project.
cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-amiens-chris.notes: The number in the Commons file name is the Gallica view number, not the folio.

cur:manuscripts-valcavado-he-cometh-with.summary: Christ, haloed and robed, stands with outstretched arms within a great swirling blue mass of cloud, flanked by angels, while below crowds of people — those who 'pierced him' and all the tribes of the earth — gesture and mourn on either side of a mound. Latin captions explain the vision.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.

Q116273823.summary: Cut into a small faceted piece of rock crystal, Christ hangs on a cross with a footrest, arms spread wide, flanked by the Virgin and Saint John, with a star and a crescent above the arms of the cross and Greek letters running down either side. Cut as an intaglio seal, it would have left a raised impression of the Crucifixion, a sign of its owner's faith. Its clarity and tiny scale make it an intimate Byzantine devotional object.
facts: The Met dates the seal broadly to the 9th–11th century and records it as rock crystal, about 2 cm high (accession 86.11.38, purchased 1886).
Q116273823.notes: The Greek letters were not read or verified.

vam:O352751.summary: Woven in red, cream, blue and green silk, this small, worn roundel shows a frontal figure with long hair and a halo, both arms raised in the ancient gesture of prayer, standing between two stylised trees. A border of floral motifs and small crosses runs round the edge. The V&A identifies the figure as Christ; it is a rare and delicate witness to Christian imagery on luxury silks of late-antique Egypt.
facts: Samite, a twill-woven silk, is thought to have originated in Sasanian Persia; Byzantine workshops adopted the technique, and it became one of the great luxury textiles of the period (V&A).
The roundel was given to the V&A by Robert Taylor in 1900; the museum dates it to about AD 500–700 and attributes it to Egypt.
vam:O352751.notes: The identification as Christ follows the V&A. The orans (praying) pose is more usual for saints, the Virgin or the deceased than for Christ, and no inscription or cross-nimbus confirms the identity, so it should be treated as uncertain.
